name: Sodium lactate
lead: Sodium lactate is the sodium salt of lactic acid (formula C3H5NaO3), a white powder or colourless syrupy liquid with a mild saline taste. It is made by fermenting a sugar source such as corn or beets and neutralising the resulting lactic acid.[1]

In personal care it works as a humectant, an ingredient that attracts and holds water in a product and on the surface of skin or hair, and as a pH-regulating salt. That is how it contributes to appearance: shampoos and liquid soaps that contain it are formulated to leave hair and skin feeling softer and less dried out, and lactate-based buffers help keep a formula at a skin-compatible acidity.[1][2][11]

Outside cosmetics it is a food additive (E325) acting as preservative, acidity regulator and bulking agent, and in medicine it is a component of Ringer's lactate solution, which is on the World Health Organization's list of essential medicines.[1][10] It does not contain milk protein.[1] Published clinical studies of sodium lactate address medical questions rather than appearance.

paras: Sodium lactate is the salt formed when lactic acid is neutralised with a sodium base. It is highly water soluble and is sold either as a white powder or as a syrup of roughly 60 percent concentration, which stays liquid at room temperature.[1] It is not chemically related to lactose, the milk sugar, despite the similar-sounding name.[1]

Commercial lactic acid is most often produced by fermenting plant-derived sugars such as maize starch, beets, potatoes or molasses. Only rarely is it fermented from dairy sources such as whey, and acid made that way generally goes back into dairy products.[1] Because of this, the ingredient does not contain milk protein, and the Wikipedia entry notes that people with milk allergy or lactose intolerance do not need to avoid it on that account.[1]

In food it serves as a preservative, acidity regulator and bulking agent, and is sold as a liquid or powder under the code E325.[1] Grokipedia states it is used against Listeria in meat products and is generally recognised as safe by the US FDA; this is AI-generated text.[2]

It is used in shampoos and liquid soaps as a humectant and moisturizer.[1] Humectants in general are hydrophilic ingredients that draw water into the outer layer of the skin or onto the hair shaft; related ingredients in the same family include glycerin, urea, sorbitol and lactic acid itself.[11] Formulators also use lactate salts together with lactic acid as a buffer pair, which lets a product sit at a stable, mildly acidic pH close to that of the skin surface.[2]

For people trying to improve how their skin and hair look, the practical role is supporting: a cleanser or shampoo with a humectant is meant to leave less of the tight, dry feeling after washing, and well-hydrated skin tends to look smoother and less flaky. Grokipedia reports use of up to 10 percent in personal care products at pH of at least 3.5 and a Cosmetic Ingredient Review safety conclusion, which is unverified here.[2]

Sodium lactate is part of Ringer's lactate solution. It has been given intravenously as a bicarbonate source for mild to moderate metabolic acidosis and to treat arrhythmias from overdose of class I antiarrhythmics; it is contraindicated in lactic acidosis.[1] Ringer's lactate, also called Hartmann's solution, contains sodium, chloride, potassium, calcium and about 28 millimoles of lactate per litre, which the liver converts to bicarbonate.[10] It is used for fluid replacement after blood loss, surgery, burns and similar situations.[10]

It can induce panic attacks in people with panic disorder and has been used as a diagnostic challenge.[1] A meta-analysis comparing provocation methods found that lactate infusion raised panic attack rates in people with panic disorder far more than in healthy controls, with a larger effect than carbon dioxide inhalation.[12]

Sydney Ringer devised the original balanced saline solution in the early 1880s while studying isolated frog hearts. In the 1930s the American paediatrician Alexis Hartmann added lactate to treat acidosis, producing the solution now known as Ringer's lactate or Hartmann's solution.[10]

The older view that lactic acid builds up in working muscle and directly causes the acidosis and fatigue of hard exercise has been revisited in the physiology literature. Reviews published in 2004 and 2006 argue that lactate production slows rather than causes acidosis and that the proton release comes from ATP breakdown, a reassessment that changed how lactate is described in sports science.[8][13]

In shampoos, soaps and food it is generally regarded as a low-risk ingredient.[1][2] Intravenous sodium lactate is a medical product given under clinical supervision. It is contraindicated in lactic acidosis and can provoke panic attacks in people with panic disorder, with the Wikipedia entry citing figures of up to 72 percent of such patients affected during intravenous challenge.[1]

No studies found for cosmetic or appearance use. Registered clinical studies of sodium lactate concern medical questions such as traumatic brain injury,[3] cardiac arrest,[4] heart failure,[5] dengue shock syndrome[6] and depression.[7] The panic-provocation literature, including the 2022 meta-analysis, uses infused sodium lactate as a research tool in panic disorder.[12] Wider lactate-biology research examines exercise acidosis[8][13] and immune and tumour signalling,[9] which is not about skin.

timeline.event: Sydney Ringer develops a balanced saline solution while working on frog hearts.[10]
Alexis Hartmann adds lactate to treat acidosis, giving Ringer's lactate or Hartmann's solution.[10]
A physiology review argues lactate production does not cause exercise acidosis.[8]
Sodium lactate appears on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (21st list).[1]

card.summary: A lactic acid salt used as a humectant and pH adjuster in personal care; its medical role is better documented than any appearance effect.
card.note: Intravenous sodium lactate is a medical product and can provoke panic attacks in people with panic disorder.

quick.overview:
Sodium lactate is a mild salt of lactic acid used in shampoos, liquid soaps and some moisturizers to hold water and balance pH. It is also a food preservative and part of hospital fluids such as Ringer's lactate.
No trials were found testing it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: As a humectant it attracts and holds water in a formulation, and as a salt of a weak acid it helps buffer pH.
quick.risks: In topical and food use it is generally regarded as low-risk. Intravenous use is medical, is contraindicated in lactic acidosis, and can induce panic attacks in people with panic disorder.
